comments.author: Sairam Sundaresan
comments.comment: One thing I’d add: version the eval prompt like code, including the chat template, system message, decoding params, and parser. Without that, a “model regression” can just be an eval harness regression in disguise.

comments.author: Christoph Burseg
comments.comment: The underappreciated part is prefill speed: for agent workloads with long prompts and short outputs, it can matter more than raw output tokens/sec. I’d be curious how the setup behaves after 1,000+ calls with mixed document sizes, especially VRAM fragmentation, queueing latency, and retry rates.

comments.author: MSc Valter Eduardo
comments.comment: The hard part is not creating agents, it is keeping them discoverable, owned, tested, and cheap enough after the first demo. I like the control-plane framing because agent sprawl starts looking a lot like microservice sprawl: versioning, permissions, observability, rollback, and cost attribution become the product. How are you thinking about eval drift when the same agent changes tools, model, or memory over time?

comments.author: Shashank Thatikonda
comments.comment:
The missing layer in most AI stack diagrams is failure routing: what happens when retrieval is weak, tool calls timeout, memory is stale, or evals disagree.

That is where agentic systems stop being demos and start becoming software.

I’d add one more box after Evaluation: rollback + human review paths.
